At Fairmead we nurture the educational journeys of our young people. Our dedicated staff are committed to making learning an enjoyable experience, ensuring that every moment is a chance to make memories.
As a staff team and as a school community our core responsibility is to prepare all young people for aspirational, successful and independent futures. It is upon this solid foundation that we have constructed a curriculum that enables young people to take responsibility, show empathy and respect, develop confidence, and empowers them to realise a strong vision for their own futures.

Welcome
Fairmead School is situated on the outskirts of Yeovil in the county of Somerset. It has a wide catchment area across south Somerset and into Dorset, welcoming young people between the ages of four and sixteen.
The school currently has 151 young people on roll, and caters for autistic young people and young people with moderate learning difficulties.
The young people are safe here, as all aspects of Safeguarding practice are upheld and adhered to. This is reflected in our Learning Pathways Curriculum, where young people learn to keep themselves safe online, in the community, or who they can talk to if they feel worried.
At Fairmead we are dedicated in improving the social and emotional well-being of our young people and offer Drama and Social Interaction therapy along with Thrive and Forest School sessions.
The school community promotes British Values; through tolerance, understanding and respecting diversity. We encourage and support our young people to develop skills, understanding and knowledge so they can make informed and positive choices about their futures.
We hope that you enjoy your visit to our website and you find all the information you are looking for.
Please contact the school directly with any queries you may wish to follow up.
Thank you for visiting

About Us
Our catchment area covers South Somerset and looks something similar to this;
Our school has been a cornerstone of special education in the region for over six decades. Established in 1964, we have consistently evolved to meet the needs of students with moderate learning difficulties and children with Autism.
151 young people on roll, 105 boys and 46 girls.
67 young people in primary and 84 in secondary.
100% of young people have an Education Health Care Plan (EHCP).
50% of young people are eligible for Pupil Premium.
7.2% of young people with English as an additional language (EAL).
3% of young people are Children Looked After (in the care of the Local Authority).
Young people with an autism diagnosis
84 young people have an autism diagnosis this equates to 54%.
70% of our primary cohort have an autism diagnosis.
40% of our secondary cohort have an autism diagnosis.
We recognise that there are young people in our school who do not have a formal diagnosis (they may or may not be on a pathway or undertaking a diagnosis).
Milestones in Our History
1964: Fairmead School was founded to provide specialised education for children with learning difficulties.
2014: The school received a 'Good' rating in its Ofsted inspection, reflecting its commitment to quality education.
2021: A significant development occurred with the opening of the Sycamore Building, a £6.85 million facility funded by Somerset County Council. This expansion included six new classrooms, replacing six older ones, and added a state-of-the-art sports facility. The Princess Royal officially opened the building, marking a new chapter in the school's growth.
2024: Fairmead School celebrated its 60th anniversary with a community event featuring music, food and games - raising money for a sensory garden project.

Work Experience
Work Experience has become a real strength over the last few years with increasing numbers of young people accessing work experience placements, independently, and for longer periods of time. Our approach remains flexible and provides young people in secondary with the opportunity to start accessing individual placements from year 9 onwards. We assess this work readiness in school following our 3Ps approach and when young people are regularly demonstrating these skills they meet with our work experience coordinator to begin the next step.
Work Experience has become a real strength over the last few years with increasing numbers of young people accessing work experience placements, independently, and for longer periods of time. Our approach remains flexible and provides young people in secondary with the opportunity to start accessing individual placements from year 9 onwards. We assess this work readiness in school following our 3Ps approach and when young people are regularly demonstrating these skills they meet with our work experience coordinator to begin the next step.
Work experience placements can be for a few days, a block week or for longer periods, one or more days a week over the academic year. This approach allows us to best meet the needs of the young people and help prepare them for their future at work. Our work experience coordinator works with young people and their families to plan these placements working with the Southwest Work Experience Partnership.
Recent placements have included a care home, a gym, a café, schools, a factory, a shop, a nursery, a country park, a hairdressers and a carpentry workshop.
For all year 11 young people to leave school having taken part in at least 10 days of work experience
For as many young people as possible to take part in offsite, independent work experience
For all young people to leave Fairmead with a clear idea of the world of work and their place within it
My Journey for Work Experience - Delivered as part of a work experience assembly.
"Hi my name is Freddy and I do work experience at Birchfield primary school. I enjoy it so much. The things I do at Birchfield is scanning on the photocopier, delivering bagels and sorting files out to help the staff. I enjoy going there because it is fun and it is good to do work experience so it can give you an idea for when you are older. The best thing about it is I get my own badge saying my name on it.
I also go to forest school for my other work experience with Badgers and Deer class. I enjoy going to forest school because I want to learn new skills. I learn how to make a fire and tie ropes and cut firewood. I enjoy it so much I would like to be a forest school teacher when I am older. So, if you are year 10 or 11 go and speak to Mrs Chorley and she will help you with finding work experience you would like to do."

Allergies
Allergy-Friendly School - Keeping our young people safe
We are proud to be an allergy-friendly school, and we are committed to creating a safe environment for all young people-especially those with serious food allergies. To support this, we ask all families and staff to follow these important guidelines:
No Nuts, No Nuts Products
To protect young people with nut allergies, no nuts or nut containing products are allowed on school premises. This includes snacks and packed lunches.
Common foods that may contain nuts include:
﻿﻿Peanut butter and other nut spreads e.g. almond, cashew
﻿﻿Nutella and other chocolate-hazelnut spreads
﻿﻿Granola bars and cereal bars
﻿﻿Some chocolate and confectionery
﻿﻿Cakes, biscuits, and pastries
﻿﻿Trail mix and snack packs
﻿﻿Desserts with nut toppings
Please always check ingredient labels carefully before sending food to school.
We also ask that raw and cooked egg is not brought into school in any form. This includes:
﻿﻿Homemade Mayonnaise
Unfortunately, if any food items containing nuts (including spreads like Nutella) or raw or cooked egg that are sent into school, we will have to dispose of them and contact parents or carers to bring an alternative item for their young person to eat.
By working together, we can ensure that every young person feels safe, included, and cared for.

The School Day
School starts 8.55am
Young people can arrive from 8.40am
School finishes at 3.15pm
After School clubs finish at 4.15pm
The compulsory school day at Fairmead starts at 8:55am and finishes at 3:15pm.
This totals 31 hours and 40 minutes a week, including breaks.
Optional after-school activities are available but are not included in this total.
Young people walking with parents/carers enter through the playground gate.
Young people on school transport enter through the main gate.
All LSA’s meet young people at the gates (8.40-8.55am) to support the transition
which includes walking primary young people to their classrooms.
Upon arrival young people go straight to their classroom or classroom outside area and access meaningful transitional activities.
Registration begins at 8.55 AM (register remains open until 9:20am)
Young people wait on the playground until the bell rings at 8:55am for registration. (Dependent on weather conditions).
After the bell rings, all young people line up on the playground in their tutor groups and are greeted by their teacher and staff team.
A member of SLT will greet everyone and dismiss tutor groups.
Registration and tutor time begins at 8.55 AM (register remains open until 9:20am)
All young people are to be in their classrooms from 3pm.
If being collected by parents or carers, young people await their name to be called to come to the playground gate.
If they are travelling on school transport, they wait for their bus number to be called and then go to the main gate.

Careers days/activities
Primary Careers Days
In November 2025 to support our focus on careers across primary groups we decided to have our first Primary Careers Day, where the whole focus could be careers and jobs. We wrote to families to ask that young people bring in something from home linked to careers and this would become a focus to start the day.
During the day young people:
were able to communicate their future work preferences in a range of ways according to their own needs
had the opportunity to take part in job type activities, like pretending to be medics and bakers
had the opportunity to dress up in work uniform
played matching games linking jobs to workplaces
did pieces of art linked to their future job ideas
Following the success of the day we went on to run two more days in 2025/26 and are planning to run them termly in 2026/27.
World of Work (WOW) week - Started February 2026
For the 2025/26 academic year we decided to host a World of Work week where visitors to the school can talk to our young people about the job they do and their own work journeys. We wrote to families and the wider staff team and asked for their support in talking to young people about their own career journeys. We were lucky enough to have some really good responses with each class having 4/5 visitors spread through the week to gain some valuable insight into some different jobs and the varied work journeys towards them.
We are now planning for our second World of Work Week in the spring term.
Thales Glider Experience
Deer and Badger class took part in a national STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering and Maths) day supported by the engineering firm Thales. As part of the day the young people learnt about the theory of flight and through an online classroom, and with the resources that had been sent to the school, took part in building their own gliders.
Ivelhurst Care Home Visit
A group of young people had the opportunity to visit Ivel Hurst Care home in Yeovil to learn about career opportunities within the care sector. During the visit young people had a tour of the facilities, met and talked to staff about their different roles, spent some time with residents and helped out in the kitchen.
AIP Welding Experience
We were visited by Kim Hunt from AIP Welding who talked to young people about working in welding and how they could go about this. As part of the visit young people had the opportunity to have a go at virtual welding, using virtual reality headsets and welding torches to try out welding for themselves.
Next Step Careers Fair
In September Fairmead School hosted our Next Steps Careers Fair, in the sports hall, where a number of providers attended the school to meet our young people and talk about some of their next step options for when they finish school. All secondary and upper primary young people the opportunity to join the event. The providers were: Yeovil College, Strode College, Department of work and Pensions (Job Centre), NHS, Dorset and Somerset Air Ambulance, Able2Achieve, Somerset Works and Platform Railway Education.
Coding with Microsoft
A group of young people from secondary were lucky enough to take part in a coding workshop run by staff from Microsoft. Staff from the company came to the school to run a day long workshop. As part of the day the team from Microsoft talked about their roles at Microsoft and how these had changed over the years. We were also joined by a group of young peoples from Fiveways school to take part in the experience. Young people used micro bits that they were able to programme using a Microsoft coding platform that allowed them to make alarms, send messages, light up to sound and light inputs and many other functions.

Careers Guidance
At Fairmead school we have been using Future Smart Careers to offer our independent careers advice and guidance over the last few years. Year 10 young people are offered individual appointments during the summer term so they have the information they need in time for their year 11 annual review meetings in the following autumn. Future Smart Careers are able to hold these meeting in a variety of ways that meet the needs of our young people, supported by Fairmead staff as needed. An action plan is then written and shared with families.
Thank you again for the warm welcome and all the support I received from you and staff members when I visited Fairmead School. It was fantastic to see how well-prepared students were for their meetings with me, and what an impact your work experience programme has on their confidence and awareness of the working world. Every student was a delight to spend time with and quite a number were very well aware of the different choices they have once they leave school. It was heart-warming to see them using their reflection skills when discussing work experience and what they have learned about the world of work and their own unique skills through these opportunities. This gave them the confidence to have discussions with a person they hadn’t met before (me) and it made my work even more impactful.
Thank you once again, I hope we have the opportunity to work together again in future.

Careers Overview
At Fairmead school we prepare our young people for their futures in a number of ways to give them the best opportunities in their future studies and into the world of work. While we follow an adapted national curriculum we also have the flexibility to provide our young people with a range of opportunities to best prepare them for their future. While acknowledging that the world of work may look different across our changing cohort of young people we work with stakeholders to revise and develop pathways towards successful adult lives, where being part of the working population remains an aspiration.
Careers in the Curriculum
English
Through teaching the fundamental skills of written and verbal communication as well as the ability to extract and analyse read information young people will have the skills they need to be successful in the workplace and life. Individual career links are also possible within lessons such as completing a deep dive into a career from the reading text at the start of each new story, which has proved a really good way to immerse the students in the book from the beginning.
Mathematics
The skills taught are and should be fundamental skills required in life and work. By making the links to the use of these skills, in their lives beyond school, young people become more engaged in their learning. While making links to topics such as using time and money provide more obvious links, as young people progress through the curriculum a wider range of links is possible.
Science
Within science units specific jobs roles are highlighted that link to the unit e.g. unit on growing plants linked to the role of a gardener. Science also has linked visits and activities such as Wessex Water visit linked to water cycle and Flying Start Challenge project linking with Leonardo staff who support the teaching of aviation through science.
RSHE
A bespoke careers unit is delivered across primary and secondary with skills being developed incrementally. Learning includes understanding people go to work and earn money to recognising own skills and how they link to future careers.
Computing
Young people are taught the skills needed in the modern workplace to be confident users of a range of different types of technology including making links to specific jobs. Young people are also taught how technology can benefit them in their lives beyond work to further spark their interests.
Religious Education
By learning about different religions young people can become more considerate about the needs of others in the community and the workplace. For example, employers might have to make adaptations within the workplace to accommodate the religious practices of certain religions, such as providing somewhere to pray, or providing different food in canteens.

Young People's Progress & Outcomes
Our 2025–2026 leavers have moved on to a wide range of further education and specialist pathways that reflect their individual strengths, aspirations, and needs.
Our destination data is presented in two categories.
Destinations – This shows where young people went after leaving Fairmead, such as Yeovil College, Strode College, Taunton College, employment or other destinations.
Pathways – This shows what type of education, training or employment pathway young people moved into, including Foundation Provision, Vocational Provision, Supported Internships, Apprenticeships, employment and NEET.
Together, these categories provide a clear picture of both where our young people progressed to and the type of pathway they entered after leaving Fairmead. We are very proud of each young person’s achievements and the confidence and independence they have shown as they take their next steps into adulthood.

House Teams & Rewards
Venus
Mars
Jupiter
Saturn
Mars
were the Summer term 2 winners!
At Fairmead School, the house team system - featuring Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, plays a vital role in building a strong, supportive school community. More than just a tradition, these teams encourage teamwork, healthy competition, and a sense of belonging among young people.
Each house team represents shared values such as respect, resilience, determination, and kindness. By participating in house activities, from sports events to academic challenges, young people develop confidence, leadership skills, and positive relationships with peers across different year groups.
The house teams create an inclusive environment where every young person has a chance to shine, contribute, and feel proud of their team. Whether it’s cheering each other on or working together towards a common goal, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn reflect the spirit of Fairmead - where every effort counts and every voice matters.
Young people in Year 10 and Year 11 can stand for the positions of house captain and vice-captain. The entire school participates in the election by voting for their representatives, who will lead and support their house teams.
At Fairmead, all staff and young people are assigned to one of the four house teams.
Fairmead Points are used to recognise and celebrate positive behaviour and the values demonstrated by our young people.
Each member of staff is allocated a set number of points:
Support staff: 15 Fairmead Points each
Teachers: 30 Fairmead Points each
Whenever a Fairmead Point is awarded, it is recorded on Bromcom as a Positive Incident Report. This record will include:
The Fairmead value the young person has demonstrated
A brief explanation of how they demonstrated that value
Each week, one young person per class will receive a Special Mention Certificate. This recognises positive choices and achievements demonstrated during that week.
A Wall of Fame will be displayed in the lunch hall. The young person with the highest number of points each month will have their photo added.
At the end of each term the young people with the highest number of Fairmead points will be entered into a Golden Ticket Raffle for the chance to win a gift voucher.
At the end of the school year the top 10 young people in secondary and top 10 young people in primary with the most Fairmead points will be rewarded with a trip (e.g. beach, park).
At the end of the summer term the house with the highest total Fairmead points will receive a movie afternoon.
A Headteacher's Award is a form of recognition given by the headteacher to young people for their outstanding achievements or positive behaviours. This award can be given for various reasons, such as academic excellence, exceptional effort, or demonstrating positive values and behaviours. The award is sent home in the post to celebrate the young person’s accomplishments and encourage others to strive for similar achievements. Young people who receive this award will have their names displayed in the lunch hall.
